newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Speculation persists over Bonn-Paris EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Speculation persists over Bonn-Paris EMU talks.

text.p: A flurry of official denials failed to stem speculation on Thursday that France and Germany are negotiating to keep Italy and Spain out of the start of a single European currency.
France, Germany and Italy all denied on Wednesday that any secret deals existed to block Italy from economic and monetary union (EMU) at its planned 1999 debut.
But influential Italian business newspaper Il Sole 24 Ore reported on Thursday that Bonn and Paris were trying to reach a consensus by September on who would be a founder member of EMU.
Il Sole gave no sources but said attempts to find an "early accord" had been requested several times by Paris this year.

The newspaper had said on Wednesday a deal was taking shape between Paris and Bonn to keep Italy and Spain out of EMU's start. In Thursday's article, it noted France and Germany's denials but said negotiations were only being sketched out now.

It said the idea of bringing forward an informal selection for EMU entry had run into difficulty especially regarding Italy and Spain, as Germany was taking an intransigent stance to them which Paris had been forced to take notice of in recent weeks.

Talks were caught between the threat of a delay to EMU on the part of Germany and the lack of economic data on the state of countries' public finances, with the first reliable figures only likely to be available in August and September.

The selection process for entering EMU is due to take place in early 1998 and qualification will be based in part on countries' economic performance in 1997, including meeting key criteria on debt, inflation and budget deficit levels.

Il Sole said France's desire to balance out German predominance in EMU meant it was open to favouring guaranteed entry to Italy but it added French President Jacques Chirac was now having to consider Germany's "intransigence".
"Even the government and the Bank of France are considering the idea of starting the euro without a wide number of countries," the newspaper said.

Italy has been striving in the last year to get its public finances in shape in time to meet the tough criteria for EMU, taking steps in recent months to bring its 1997 budget deficit down to the required three percent of gross domestic product from around 6.8 percent last year.

But there have been doubts from abroad on whether its efforts will have a lasting effect beyond 1997. Many ordinary Germans, in particular, are averse to Italy's entry, fearing it would soften the euro and make it prone to inflation.

Former European Commission president Jacques Delors, interviewed in another Italian newspaper on Thursday, dismissed the idea that either German Chancellor Helmut Kohl or Chirac was involved in a deal to exclude Italy.
He told La Repubblica he was sure France wanted Italy in EMU from day one and any real problem lay with the Germans.
"Germany was convinced that only six or seven countries would take part in EMU, at least in the first phase. The idea of a larger union throws them into panic," he said.
